name: CIPA: Filters, Monitoring, and Teaching Safety
title: CIPA: Filters, Monitoring, and Teaching Safety
answer: CIPA is a federal program condition for schools that receive discounts on internet service through the Schools and Libraries Program. To get those discounts, a school must certify an internet safety policy that blocks certain harmful images, monitors minors online, and teaches students about safe online behavior. AI chat tools and image generators create new gaps in those policies, so schools need to name AI tools directly and decide which ones students may use.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: CIPA is tied to schools that get discounts on internet service through the federal Schools and Libraries Program. A school that wants those discounts has to certify an internet safety policy. That policy must use technology to block images that are obscene, show child sexual abuse, or are harmful to minors. It must also cover monitoring of minors online and teaching students about appropriate behavior, including social networking, chat rooms, and cyberbullying. Before the policy is adopted, the school must give notice and hold at least one public meeting.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, the CIPA requirements shape what a school must put in its internet safety policy and how it teaches online safety. The text does not give grade bands, so the same requirements apply across a school's policy rather than by age group. Schools should update the policy to name AI tools directly and to state which ones students may use. The teaching requirement can carry lessons on AI, including how chatbots can be wrong and how generated images can be used to hurt people. These steps sit alongside the existing duties to block harmful images, monitor minors online, and teach appropriate behavior.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text supports the CIPA requirements with a citation to the New Jersey School Boards Association, n.d. It does not present a study, figure, or finding. The AI-specific points are framed as new questions and recommended updates, not as research results. So the CIPA duties rest on the cited policy guidance, while the AI guidance rests on practice and policy judgment rather than research evidence.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text warns that a filter built to block websites may not catch what a chatbot says inside an approved app. Image generators can produce harmful content that no filter has seen before. Schools should update their internet safety policy to name AI tools directly and to say which ones students may use. The teaching requirement is a natural place for lessons on how chatbots can be wrong and how generated images can be used to hurt people. Decisions about which AI tools students may use stay with the school through its policy.
